concept.name: Zero Trust Networking

relationships.description: Connects Zero Trust Networking to api security oauth2 in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Zero-trust networking replaces implicit IP- and VLAN-based perimeter trust with cryptographic workload identity (SPIFFE/mTLS), continuous device/user attestation, and per-request L7 authorization (Envoy/OPA) on every hop.
spark.keyTakeaway: Never trust a packet because it arrived on a private RFC 1918 subnet; authenticate every caller's short-lived X.509 SVID over mTLS and authorize the exact HTTP/gRPC action on every service boundary.

concept.whyItMatters: Traditional castle-and-moat networks assume anything inside `10.0.0.0/8` is benign. Once an attacker compromises a single CI runner, SSRF-vulnerable pod, or developer laptop over VPN, flat internal networks allow unconstrained lateral movement to databases and KMS endpoints. In ephemeral Kubernetes and multi-cloud clusters where pod IPs recycle every few minutes, IP allowlists are both operationally brittle and security-blind—only cryptographic identity scales.
whenToUse: Multi-tenant or regulated microservices (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, SOC 2) in Kubernetes/ECS where lateral movement after a single pod compromise must be blocked by default-deny L7 policies.
Hybrid or multi-cloud architectures (e.g., AWS EKS calling on-prem Postgres or GCP Cloud Run) where traffic traverses untrusted WANs without relying on brittle site-to-site IPsec tunnels.
Remote engineering access to internal admin panels, CI/CD, and production APIs via Identity-Aware Proxies (Cloudflare Access, Google BeyondCorp IAP, Tailscale) instead of broad corporate VPNs.
whenNotToUse: Ultra-low-latency (<100 microsecond) IPC or kernel-bypass HPC/HFT fabrics (RDMA/DPDK) inside a physically isolated single-tenant rack where per-packet TLS/sidecar proxy hops blow the latency budget.
Legacy embedded OT/SCADA hardware incapable of TLS 1.3 or short-lived certificate rotation, which must instead be isolated behind terminating zero-trust gateways.
Single-process monoliths or isolated dev sandboxes where adding a full SPIRE + Envoy control plane introduces operational complexity without meaningful trust boundaries.
keyPoints: Every workload receives a cryptographic identity—typically a SPIFFE ID (`spiffe://prod.internal/ns/payments/sa/ledger-api`) encoded in a short-lived X.509 SVID (1-hour to 24-hour TTL) rotated automatically without restarts.
Transport encryption and mutual authentication (mTLS via TLS 1.3) ensure both client and server verify each other's certificates before exchanging a single application byte.
Authorization is evaluated per request at L7 (Envoy RBAC, OPA/Rego, or Cilium eBPF) using `(caller_spiffe_id, user_jwt_claims, method, path)`—not source IP or CIDR blocks.
User-to-service access uses Identity-Aware Proxies (OIDC/OAuth2 + device posture/TPM attestation) so compromised credentials on an unmanaged device are still rejected.
Default-deny network posture: services reject all unauthenticated or unauthorized RPCs, and egress proxies restrict outbound calls to explicitly allowlisted domains/APIs.

examples.title: Stopping Lateral Movement in Kubernetes with SPIRE + Envoy mTLS
examples.scenario: An attacker exploits a deserialization CVE in a public-facing `frontend-web` pod (`10.24.8.19`) and attempts to query `ledger-db-proxy:5432` and `kms-signer:8443` directly from a shell inside the pod.
examples.outcome: The pod only holds the `spiffe://prod/ns/web/sa/frontend` SVID. `ledger-db-proxy` terminates TLS 1.3 mTLS, inspects the SAN URI, and rejects the handshake/L7 request (`403 RBAC: access denied`) because only `spiffe://prod/ns/payments/sa/checkout` is authorized—containing the breach to the frontend pod.

examples.title: Replacing Corporate VPN with BeyondCorp Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)
examples.scenario: A 400-engineer company retires its OpenVPN concentrator, which previously granted every authenticated employee L3 access to the entire `10.100.0.0/16` production VPC.
examples.outcome: Engineers access internal Grafana, ArgoCD, and admin tools through an OIDC-backed IAP requiring hardware FIDO2 MFA and CrowdStrike/MDM disk-encryption posture checks. Each session receives a 15-minute signed JWT assertion, cutting lateral attack surface by >95%.

tradeOffs.factor: Sidecar Proxy (Envoy/Istio) vs. Ambient / Kernel eBPF (Cilium)
tradeOffs.pro: Sidecars enforce rich L7 HTTP/gRPC RBAC, JWT validation, and per-RPC telemetry uniformly across any language.
tradeOffs.con: Adds ~1–2 ms p99 latency per hop and ~50–100 MB RAM + 0.05–0.15 vCPU per pod; ambient/eBPF modes cut memory by moving L4 mTLS to node-level ztunnel/kernel.

tradeOffs.factor: Short-Lived SVIDs (1h TTL) vs. Long-Lived Certs + CRL/OCSP
tradeOffs.pro: Eliminates brittle CRL/OCSP revocation lookups on the hot path—stolen certs expire automatically within 60 minutes.
tradeOffs.con: Requires a highly available, low-latency local SDS/SPIRE Agent on every node; if the CA control plane stalls for >1h, workloads lose valid certs simultaneously.

tradeOffs.factor: Strict Default-Deny Policy vs. Developer Velocity
tradeOffs.pro: Prevents shadow APIs and accidental over-privileged service-to-service paths from reaching production.
tradeOffs.con: New microservice integrations fail with `403` until explicit `AuthorizationPolicy` manifests are reviewed and deployed in CI/CD.

failureModes.name: Mesh-Wide Certificate Expiry Outage
failureModes.description: The root/intermediate CA (SPIRE Server or Istiod) fails to rotate intermediate signing keys or nodes lose connectivity to the CA for longer than the SVID TTL (e.g., 1–24 hours), causing all mTLS handshakes across the cluster to fail simultaneously.
failureModes.mitigation: Monitor `cert_expiry_seconds_remaining` with alerts at 50% TTL, configure overlapping rotation at 50% lifetime, run HA multi-AZ CA replicas, and keep intermediate TTLs (7–30 days) well above workload SVID TTLs (1–24h).

failureModes.name: Confused Deputy via Unvalidated JWT / Header Forwarding
failureModes.description: Service A authenticates over mTLS to Service B and forwards a user's `X-User-Id` header or unverified JWT; Service B trusts the header without verifying the JWT signature or restricting which callers may assert user context.
failureModes.mitigation: Strip untrusted `X-User-*` headers at the edge proxy, validate signed OIDC/JWT tokens at every L7 hop (or mint short-lived actor/delegation tokens), and bind L7 RBAC to both caller SPIFFE ID and JWT `aud`/`sub` claims.

failureModes.name: Policy Engine Bottleneck on the Hot Path
failureModes.description: Every Envoy proxy makes a synchronous network call to a centralized OPA cluster for authorization, adding 15–40 ms tail latency and turning an OPA outage into a full site outage.
failureModes.mitigation: Compile Rego policies into local Wasm or Envoy-native `RBAC` filters evaluated in-process (<0.5 ms), or co-locate OPA as a node/pod sidecar with fail-closed/cached bundle sync.

failureModes.name: Clock Skew Breaking Short-Lived SVID & JWT Validation
failureModes.description: A VM or bare-metal node drifts >5 minutes behind UTC, causing it to reject newly minted SVIDs (`notBefore` in the future) and expired JWTs.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce Chrony/PTP time sync across all nodes, alert on >500 ms drift, and backdate SVID `notBefore` by 30–60 seconds during issuance.

commonMistakes: Terminating TLS at the ingress/API gateway and running plaintext HTTP inside the cluster (`PERMISSIVE` mTLS mode left on indefinitely), leaving internal traffic exposed to sniffing and spoofing.
Using IP-based `NetworkPolicy` alone without L7 workload identity—IPs are reused rapidly in Kubernetes and cannot distinguish two tenants or two endpoints on the same host.
Granting wildcard authorization (`principals: ["*"]` or `methods: ["*"]`) to unblock a deploy and never scoping it down to least-privilege `(spiffe_id, method, path)`.
Forgetting egress controls—allowing compromised pods to open arbitrary outbound TCP/DNS tunnels to attacker C2 servers.
Neglecting emergency break-glass runbooks when the OIDC provider or SPIRE server is unreachable during an incident.

sections.content:
## The idea

Per **NIST SP 800-207**, zero-trust networking starts from a single premise: **network location does not imply trust**. Whether a packet originates from a coffee-shop Wi-Fi, a corporate office LAN, or `10.42.0.15` inside your own Kubernetes VPC, it is treated as untrusted until proven otherwise.

Instead of defending a static IP perimeter, zero trust binds security to **cryptographic identity** and **per-request context**:
1. **Workload Identity (SPIFFE/SPIRE)**: Every service instance proves who it is via node/platform attestation (AWS IID, K8s projected ServiceAccount token, or hardware TPM 2.0) and receives a short-lived X.509 certificate (SVID) encoding its canonical URI (`spiffe://trust-domain/ns/payments/sa/checkout`).
2. **Mutual TLS (mTLS)**: Both caller and callee present and verify SVIDs over TLS 1.3, guaranteeing confidentiality, integrity, and mutual authentication on every hop.
3. **Policy Decision & Enforcement (PDP/PEP)**: An in-line Policy Enforcement Point (Envoy proxy or Identity-Aware Proxy) evaluates each request against least-privilege rules combining *who* the caller is (SPIFFE ID), *who* the end-user is (verified OIDC JWT), and *what* action is requested (`POST /v1/refunds`).

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace an engineer triggering a refund via an internal support tool (`https://support.corp.internal`) backed by `support-bff` -> `payments-api` in Kubernetes:

1. **User & Device Attestation**: The engineer's browser hits the **Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)**. IAP redirects to the OIDC IdP, verifies a hardware FIDO2 passkey plus MDM device-posture claim (`disk_encrypted=true, os_patched=true`), and attaches a 15-minute signed JWT (`sub=alice@corp.com, role=support_l2`) before forwarding to `support-bff`.
2. **Workload Identity Issuance**: On the Kubernetes worker node, the local **SPIRE Agent** attests `support-bff`'s pod UID and projected ServiceAccount token against the Kubelet, then delivers a 1-hour X.509 SVID (`spiffe://prod.corp/ns/support/sa/support-bff`) over a Unix domain socket via Envoy SDS.
3. **mTLS Handshake**: `support-bff` calls `https://payments-api.prod.svc:8443/v1/refunds`. Its local Envoy sidecar initiates TLS 1.3 mTLS with `payments-api`'s Envoy sidecar. Both sides validate the SPIFFE trust-bundle root CA and SAN URI (`~1.4 ms` new handshake, `<0.1 ms` on pooled HTTP/2 connection).
4. **L7 Policy Evaluation**: `payments-api`'s Envoy PEP inspects the verified peer SPIFFE ID (`support-bff`), the forwarded OIDC JWT (`role=support_l2`), and the HTTP route (`POST /v1/refunds`). Its compiled RBAC/OPA rule (`allow if peer == support-bff AND jwt.role in ['support_l2', 'finance']`) passes in `0.3 ms` and forwards the request to the `payments-api` container over `localhost`.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Workload identity, mTLS, and policy enforcement
sections.content:
## Workload identity, mTLS, and policy enforcement

A production zero-trust fabric separates **identity issuance** from **policy enforcement**:

- **SPIFFE / SPIRE**: Solves the "secret zero" problem—how a freshly booted container gets its first credential without baking static API keys into images. SPIRE verifies platform-native signals (AWS EC2 instance identity documents signed by AWS, GCP instance metadata JWTs, or Kubernetes projected ServiceAccount tokens) before minting an X.509 SVID with a 1-hour lifetime.
- **mTLS & Connection Pooling**: TLS 1.3 reduces full handshakes to 1 RTT (`~1–2 ms` intra-region). By keeping HTTP/2 or gRPC connections pooled between Envoy sidecars, subsequent RPCs amortize handshake cost to near zero while retaining per-stream L7 authorization.
- **Defense in Depth (L4 + L7)**: Pair kernel eBPF/CNI `NetworkPolicy` (blocking unexpected ports like SSH/22 or direct DB access) with L7 Envoy/OPA policies (restricting `GET /users/*` vs. `DELETE /users/*`), since L4 firewalls alone cannot inspect HTTP verbs or JWT claims.

## Zero-trust enforcement models compared

| Architecture | Identity Mechanism | Encryption Layer | Policy Granularity | Latency & Resource Cost |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Sidecar Mesh (Istio / Envoy)** | SPIFFE X.509 SVID via SDS | TLS 1.3 mTLS per pod | Full L7 (HTTP/gRPC verb, path, JWT) | +1–2 ms p99; ~60–100 MB RAM/pod |
| **Ambient / Node Proxy + eBPF (Cilium / Istio Ambient)** | SPIFFE SVID per node/SA | WireGuard or node ztunnel mTLS | L4 in kernel; optional L7 waypoint | <0.5 ms L4; 5–10x lower RAM than sidecars |
| **Identity-Aware Proxy (BeyondCorp / Cloudflare Access)** | OIDC + Device MDM + FIDO2 | TLS 1.3 edge termination | User/group + device posture + URL | +5–15 ms at edge; zero pod sidecars |
| **Traditional IPsec VPN + Security Groups** | Static CIDR / IP + shared PSK | L3 tunnel to VPC perimeter | L3/L4 IP & port only | Weakest: flat lateral trust once inside VPC |

## Failure modes

- **CA outage exceeding SVID TTL**: If SPIRE Server / Istiod is down longer than the 1-hour SVID lifetime, rotating certificates fail and all east-west mTLS traffic collapses simultaneously.
- **Permissive mode drift**: Teams enable `mTLS: PERMISSIVE` during migration and forget to flip to `STRICT`, allowing unauthenticated plaintext lateral movement.
- **Header spoofing (Confused Deputy)**: Backends trust `X-Forwarded-User` headers from any mTLS peer without validating who is allowed to assert end-user identity.
- **Centralized PDP latency/outage**: Making synchronous remote calls to an external OPA server on every RPC turns policy evaluation into a single point of failure.

## Operational sizing & rotation math

Two quantitative rules keep a zero-trust mesh reliable at scale:

1. **Certificate Rotation Budget**: With 10,000 pods and a 1-hour SVID TTL rotated at 50% lifetime (`30 min`), the CA signs `10,000 / 1,800s ≈ 5.6 CSRs/sec` steady-state—but during a simultaneous node-pool scale-up of 2,000 pods, burst signing hits `300+ CSRs/sec`. Size SPIRE/Istiod CPU for 10x burst CSR signing and set `cert_rotation_jitter` to prevent thundering herds.
2. **mTLS CPU & Memory Overhead**: At 50,000 RPS across Envoy sidecars using AES-128-GCM (hardware AES-NI) and pooled HTTP/2 connections, TLS framing adds `~3–6%` CPU, while Envoy connection buffers and xDS config consume `~60–120 MB` RSS per pod (rising to `300+ MB` if cluster-wide `Sidecar` egress scoping is omitted).

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Enforce `STRICT` TLS 1.3 mTLS across all production namespaces; verify zero plaintext listeners remain.
- [ ] Issue short-lived workload SVIDs (1–24h TTL) via SPIRE or mesh CA with automatic rotation at 50% lifetime and 500 ms max NTP/Chrony clock skew.
- [ ] Scope Envoy `Sidecar` / `AuthorizationPolicy` manifests to explicit `(caller_spiffe_id, method, path)` tuples—never `principals: ["*"]`.
- [ ] Validate OIDC/JWT signatures and strip untrusted `X-User-*` headers at the edge and service boundaries.
- [ ] Run OPA/RBAC evaluation in-process (Envoy native RBAC or Wasm) rather than synchronous remote PDP calls.
- [ ] Lock down pod egress with default-deny egress proxies and maintain a documented break-glass runbook for IdP/CA outages.

interviewProblems.title: Zero Trust Networking
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Zero Trust Networking. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Zero-trust networking replaces implicit IP- and VLAN-based perimeter trust with cryptographic workload identity (SPIFFE/mTLS), continuous device/user attestation, and per-request L7 authorization (Envoy/OPA) on every hop.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: SPIRE Control Plane applies the primary invariant and coordinates with payments-api + Envoy.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, payments-api + Envoy experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Monitor `cert_expiry_seconds_remaining` with alerts at 50% TTL, configure overlapping rotation at 50% lifetime, run HA multi-AZ CA replicas, and keep intermediate TTLs (7–30 days) well above workload SVID TTLs (1–24h).

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Never trust a packet because it arrived on a private RFC 1918 subnet; authenticate every caller's short-lived X.509 SVID over mTLS and authorize the exact HTTP/gRPC action on every service boundary.

Avoid trap: Terminating TLS at the ingress/API gateway and running plaintext HTTP inside the cluster (`PERMISSIVE` mTLS mode left on indefinitely), leaving internal traffic exposed to sniffing and spoofing.
Avoid trap: Using IP-based `NetworkPolicy` alone without L7 workload identity—IPs are reused rapidly in Kubernetes and cannot distinguish two tenants or two endpoints on the same host.

When to reach for it: Multi-tenant or regulated microservices (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, SOC 2) in Kubernetes/ECS where lateral movement after a single pod compromise must be blocked by default-deny L7 policies.

When to reach for it: Hybrid or multi-cloud architectures (e.g., AWS EKS calling on-prem Postgres or GCP Cloud Run) where traffic traverses untrusted WANs without relying on brittle site-to-site IPsec tunnels.

putItTogether.title: Putting Zero Trust Networking Together
putItTogether.summary: Never trust a packet because it arrived on a private RFC 1918 subnet; authenticate every caller's short-lived X.509 SVID over mTLS and authorize the exact HTTP/gRPC action on every service boundary.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Zero Trust Networking before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: The pod only holds the `spiffe://prod/ns/web/sa/frontend` SVID. `ledger-db-proxy` terminates TLS 1.3 mTLS, inspects the SAN URI, and rejects the handshake/L7 request (`403 RBAC: access denied`) because only `spiffe://prod/ns/payments/sa/checkout` is authorized—containing the breach to the frontend pod.
